concepts.title: What Was Covered in the Session
concepts.text_md:
The session included a complete beginner-friendly hands-on workflow:

1. Install Git
2. Configure Git for the first time
3. Create a GitHub account
4. Create a GitHub repository
5. Clone a repository
6. Create and modify files
7. Check changes using `git status`
8. Stage changes using `git add`
9. Save changes using `git commit`
10. Push changes to GitHub using `git push`
11. View commit history using `git log`
12. Understand how `git revert` can be used to undo changes safely

The session also discussed the importance of a **GitHub profile** for:

- 💼 Job interviews
- 🌐 Open-source contributions
- 📂 Project portfolios
- 🤝 Collaboration
- 📈 Demonstrating practical development experience

Security and collaboration topics included:

- 🔐 Public vs Private repositories
- 🛡️ Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
- 🔒 Branch protection
- 👥 Repository access and collaboration
- 🌍 Open-source contribution

The session concluded with a brief introduction to **AWS, Azure, and GCP**, explaining where cloud platforms fit into the DevOps lifecycle and how Git can integrate with CI/CD tools.

concepts.title: Git Workflow
concepts.text_md:
The basic workflow demonstrated in the session:

```text
        Install Git
            │
            ▼
   Create GitHub Account
            │
            ▼
    Create Repository
            │
            ▼
      Clone Repository
            │
            ▼
        Create Files
            │
            ▼
       git status
            │
            ▼
         git add
            │
            ▼
        git commit
            │
            ▼
         git push
            │
            ▼
   Code Available on GitHub
```

### 🧩 Git's Basic Working Model

```text
Working Directory
       │
       │ git add
       ▼
Staging Area
       │
       │ git commit
       ▼
Local Repository
       │
       │ git push
       ▼
Remote Repository
     (GitHub)
```

concepts.title: Check Git Version
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git --version
```

Used to verify that Git is installed and available from the command line.

concepts.title: Configure Git Username
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
```

concepts.title: Configure Git Email
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
```

These settings identify the author of commits created from the configured Git environment.

concepts.title: Initialize a Repository
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git init
```

Creates a new Git repository in the current project directory.

concepts.title: Clone a Repository
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git clone <repository-url>
```

Creates a local copy of an existing remote repository.

concepts.title: Check Repository Status
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git status
```

Shows the current state of files in the working directory and staging area.

concepts.title: Stage Changes
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git add .
```

Stages the changes so they can be included in the next commit.

concepts.title: Create a Commit
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git commit -m "First Commit"
```

Creates a commit containing the staged changes.

> 💡 **Best Practice:** Use meaningful commit messages so other developers can understand what changed.

concepts.title: Push Changes
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git push
```

Uploads committed local changes to the remote repository.

concepts.title: View Commit History
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git log
```

Displays the commit history of the repository.

concepts.title: Revert a Commit
concepts.text_md:
```bash
git revert <commit-id>
```

Creates a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by an earlier commit.

concepts.title: Key Takeaway
concepts.text_md:
> **Git tracks and manages your code history. GitHub provides a platform to host, share, collaborate on, and showcase that Git-based work.**

The most important Day-1 workflow to remember is:

```text
Create / Modify Code
        ↓
    git status
        ↓
      git add
        ↓
    git commit
        ↓
     git push
        ↓
      GitHub
```

Understanding this workflow gives you the foundation required for the more advanced Git and GitHub practices used in real-world DevOps teams.

questions.title: What is a Version Control System (VCS), and why is it important?
questions.prompt: What is a Version Control System (VCS), and why is it important?
questions.reference_answer: A Version Control System tracks changes made to files and maintains their history. It helps developers collaborate, understand what changed, recover previous versions, and manage source code efficiently.

questions.title: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.reference_answer: Git** is a distributed version control system used to track changes locally. **GitHub** is a cloud-based platform used to host Git repositories and support collaboration, sharing, and project management.

questions.title: Why is Git called a Distributed Version Control System?
questions.prompt: Why is Git called a Distributed Version Control System?
questions.reference_answer: Git is called distributed because each developer's local repository contains the project's version history. Developers can perform many Git operations locally without depending on a central server.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the .git directory?
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the .git directory?
questions.reference_answer: The `.git` directory contains the repository's Git metadata and information required for version control, including repository history and configuration information.

questions.title: What is the difference between git clone and git init?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between git clone and git init?
questions.reference_answer:
| `git clone` | `git init` |
|---|---|
| Creates a local copy of an existing repository | Initializes a new Git repository |
| Usually used with an existing remote repository | Used when starting Git tracking in a local project |
| Downloads the existing repository history | Creates the local `.git` repository structure |

questions.title: What is the purpose of git status?
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of git status?
questions.reference_answer: `git status` shows the current state of the working directory and staging area. It helps identify modified, untracked, and staged files.

questions.title: What is a commit, and why should commit messages be meaningful?
questions.prompt: What is a commit, and why should commit messages be meaningful?
questions.reference_answer: A commit records staged changes in the Git repository. Meaningful commit messages make the project history easier for developers to understand and maintain.

questions.title: What is the difference between a Public Repository and a Private Repository?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a Public Repository and a Private Repository?
questions.reference_answer:
Public Repository:** Can be viewed publicly on GitHub.
- **Private Repository:** Access is restricted to authorized users.

Companies generally use repository visibility and access controls according to the sensitivity of their source code and project requirements.

questions.title: Why do recruiters often ask for your GitHub profile?
questions.prompt: Why do recruiters often ask for your GitHub profile?
questions.reference_answer: A GitHub profile can demonstrate practical development experience through projects, repositories, commit history, collaboration, and open-source contributions. It can act as a technical portfolio alongside a resume.

questions.title: Joining an Existing Project
questions.prompt: Which Git command will you use first, and why?
questions.reference_answer:
I would use:

```bash
git clone <repository-url>
```

This creates a local copy of the existing GitHub repository so I can work on the project locally.

questions.title: Recovering a Deleted File
questions.prompt: How can Git help you recover the previous version?
questions.reference_answer:
Git maintains the project's version history. I would inspect the repository history and identify the required previous version or commit, then restore the required file or changes from that history.

The important point is that Git provides a history of changes, which can help recover earlier versions.

questions.title: Project Exists on GitHub
questions.prompt: How will you start working on the project?
questions.reference_answer:
```bash
git clone <repository-url>
```

After cloning, I would move into the project directory and begin working on the local copy.

questions.title: Consistent Git Identity
questions.prompt: Which Git configuration commands will you use?
questions.reference_answer:
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
```

These configure the name and email associated with commits created from that Git environment.

questions.title: New Local Project
questions.prompt: What steps will you perform before pushing the project to GitHub?
questions.reference_answer:
```bash
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
```

Then I would connect the local repository to the appropriate remote GitHub repository and push the committed changes.

questions.title: Showcasing Development Work
questions.prompt: How would you use GitHub to showcase your projects and contributions?
questions.reference_answer: I would maintain a professional GitHub profile containing relevant projects, clear repository names, useful `README.md` files, meaningful commit history, and public repositories where appropriate. I would also highlight relevant open-source contributions.

questions.title: Restricting Source Code Access
questions.prompt: Which GitHub repository settings would you recommend?
questions.reference_answer: I would use a **Private Repository** and configure access so that only authorized team members can access it. I would also use appropriate repository security and branch protection settings based on the team's requirements.

questions.title: Open-Source Contribution
questions.prompt: Which GitHub feature will you use, and what is the typical workflow?
questions.reference_answer:
I would use a **fork** of the repository.

A typical workflow is:

```text
Original Repository
        ↓
       Fork
        ↓
Your GitHub Repository
        ↓
     Clone Locally
        ↓
   Make Changes
        ↓
      Commit
        ↓
       Push
        ↓
 Pull Request
        ↓
Original Repository
```

questions.title: Teammate Cannot See Local Changes
questions.prompt: What steps might you have missed?
questions.reference_answer:
I would check whether I:

1. Saved the files.
2. Checked the changes with `git status`.
3. Staged the changes using `git add`.
4. Created a commit using `git commit`.
5. Pushed the commit using `git push`.

The key point is that **local changes are not automatically available on GitHub**. They need to be committed and pushed.

questions.title: Securing Source Code
questions.prompt: Which GitHub security features would you enable?
questions.reference_answer:
Based on the session, I would consider:

- 🔐 Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
- 🔒 Private repositories where required
- 🛡️ Branch protection
- 👥 Controlled repository access
- 🔑 Appropriate permissions for team members

The goal is to ensure that only authorized users can access or modify sensitive source code.
